publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: five categories of plant biostimulant - microbial inoculants, humic acids, fulvic acids, protein hydrolysates and amino acids, seaweed extracts
span.quote: Scope This article describes the emerging definitions of biostimulants and reviews the literature on five categories of biostimulants: i. microbial inoculants, ii. humic acids, iii. fulvic acids, iv. protein hydrolysates and amino acids, and v. seaweed extracts.

span.label: what the refereed literature actually supports for each category of biostimulant, given definitions supplied by industry consortia
span.quote: The overall aim of the review is to begin a critical review of selected refereed scientific publications, that report effects of the various categories of plant biostimulants arising from the definitions and descriptions of biostimulants that are included in the European and North American biostimulant consortia.

span.label: a critical review organised by the two consortium definitions, reporting a common response profile across chemically unrelated inputs
span.quote: The cited literature also reveals some commonalities in plant responses to different biostimulants, such as increased root growth, enhanced nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Despite the growing use of biostimulants in agriculture, many in the scientific comm unity consider biostimulants to be lacking peer-reviewed scientific evaluation.

span.label: enhancement of plant growth by substances and microorganisms that are neither fertilisers nor pesticides
span.quote: “Plant biostimulants contain substance(s) and/or microorganisms whose function when applied to plants or the rhizosphere is to stimulate natural processes to enhance/ benefit nutrient uptake, nutrient efficiency, tolerance to abiotic stress, and crop quality. Biostimulants have no direct action against pests, and therefore do not fall within the regulatory framework of pesticides” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012a).

span.label: critical review of refereed publications, category by category, building on du Jardin's bibliographic analysis
span.term: critical review of refereed publications, category by category, building on du Jardin's bibliographic analysis
span.quote: This analysis listed the major claims for the references found in data bases for each category of biostimulant. The current review builds on the analysis of du Jardin (2012).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE EUROPEAN BOUNDARY IS REGULATORY, NOT BIOLOGICAL: the definition excludes direct action against pests, which is what keeps biostimulants outside the pesticide framework rather than any claim about how they work
span.quote: “Plant biostimulants contain substance(s) and/or microorganisms whose function when applied to plants or the rhizosphere is to stimulate natural processes to enhance/ benefit nutrient uptake, nutrient efficiency, tolerance to abiotic stress, and crop quality. Biostimulants have no direct action against pests, and therefore do not fall within the regulatory framework of pesticides” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012a).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE NORTH AMERICAN BOUNDARY IS A CLAIM RESTRICTION: a biostimulant may enhance the plant's ability to assimilate nutrients but may make no nutrient claim, so the line is drawn at what may be asserted on the label
span.quote: In North America, the biostimulant coalition defined biostimulants as “substances, including microorganisms, that are applied to plant, seed, soil or other growing media that may enhance the plant’s ability to assimilate applied nutrients, or provide benefits to plant development. Biostimulants are not plant nutrients and therefore may not make any nutrient claims or guarantees” (Biostimulant 2013).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A COMMON RESPONSE PROFILE ACROSS UNRELATED INPUTS: five categories with nothing chemical in common are reported to produce the same three effects - increased root growth, enhanced nutrient uptake, stress tolerance
span.quote: The cited literature also reveals some commonalities in plant responses to different biostimulants, such as increased root growth, enhanced nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance.

span.label: four named routes by which an inoculant promotes growth: asymbiotic nitrogen fixation, nutrient solubilisation, iron sequestration by siderophores, and volatile organic compounds
span.quote: Several mechanisms have been reported for how specific microbial inoculants stimulate plant growth and nutrient uptake, including (i) asymbiotic nitrogen fixation (Boddey and Dobereiner 1995; Döbereiner 1997), (ii) solubilization of nutrients (de Freitas et al. 1997), (iii) sequestering of iron by production of siderophores, and (iv) production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

span.label: organic acids free bound phosphate two ways at once - their hydroxyl and carboxyl groups chelate the cations holding it, and they lower the surrounding soil pH
span.quote: Organic acids transform insoluble phosphate forms to soluble forms through their hydroxyl and carboxyl groups.

span.label: which organic acid a microbe releases depends on the species, so the solubilising mechanism is strain-specific rather than generic
span.quote: The type of organic acid released by a microorganism depends on the species of the microorganism.

span.label: phosphorus fertiliser can be present and still unavailable because it binds to soil particles - the problem is chemical form, not quantity
span.quote: Even when P fertilizers are added to soils, they may not be absorbed by plants 6 Plant Soil (2014) 383:3–41 because P is readily bound to soil particles, thereby being unavailable for plants (Gyaneshwar et al. 2002).

span.label: The definition of the review's own object is stated to be UNSETTLED - still evolving, and partly because the inputs it covers have little in common
span.quote: The definition and concept of plant biostimulants is still evolving, which is partly a reflection of the diversity of inputs that can be considered to be biostimulants.

span.label: The field's evidence base is described by the paper itself as widely considered to lack peer-reviewed scientific evaluation
span.note: about this quote: the quote carries a spurious space inside a word (taxonomy shape 8): the paper's “community” is staged as “comm unity”. Verbatim against the staged text; the sentence cannot be re-sliced around it because the damage is mid-clause. Confidence 0.85 under Q-606.
span.quote: Despite the growing use of biostimulants in agriculture, many in the scientific comm unity consider biostimulants to be lacking peer-reviewed scientific evaluation.

span.label: The review's scope is INHERITED from two industry consortia rather than set by the authors - what counts as a biostimulant here is what EBIC and the biostimulant coalition say it is
span.quote: The overall aim of the review is to begin a critical review of selected refereed scientific publications, that report effects of the various categories of plant biostimulants arising from the definitions and descriptions of biostimulants that are included in the European and North American biostimulant consortia.

span.label: The combination of categories, which the paper names as the obvious next step, is offered as theoretical - no combined trial is reviewed
span.quote: An obvious area for future research and development of biostimulants is the combination of some of the various categories presented in this review. For example, combinations of microbial inoculants with seaweed extracts or humic substances could theoretically deliver more reproducible benefits to crop production.

span.label: nitrogen fixation does NOT account for all the growth promotion attributed to Azospirillum - stated plainly against the mechanism the genus is famous for
span.quote: It should be noted however that nitrogen fixation does not account for all of the observed growth promotion noted with the use of Azospirillum species.

span.label: the plant species or cultivar can itself decide whether a biofertilizer produces any benefit
span.quote: For example, the species and variety of plant can sometimes be a determining factor in obtaining benefits using biofertilizers (Dalmastri et al. 1999; Remans et al. 2008).

span.label: effects must be tested for reproducibility across a range of soil types and environmental conditions before an inoculant can be relied on
span.quote: Reproducibility of effects of microbial inoculants needs to be tested across a range of soil types and environmental conditions.

span.label: the organism has to survive the commercial formulation and stay compatible with the fertilisers and crop protection chemicals already in use
span.quote: The inoculated microorganisms must survive in the selected formulation and produce the desired activity following inoculation in the field.

span.label: stressed plants grown with and without humic acid, with abscisic acid measured in both
span.note: eliminates: the stress response itself as the explanation - ABA is similar in both, so what humic acid changes is not the plant's stress signalling
span.quote: However, abscisic acid (ABA) levels were similar in stressed plants with and without humic acid.

span.label: plant biostimulants
span.quote: “Plant biostimulants contain substance(s) and/or microorganisms whose function when applied to plants or the rhizosphere is to stimulate natural processes to enhance/ benefit nutrient uptake, nutrient efficiency, tolerance to abiotic stress, and crop quality. Biostimulants have no direct action against pests, and therefore do not fall within the regulatory framework of pesticides” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012a).

span.label: EBIC
span.quote: In Europe, the EBIC defined plant biostimulants as follows. “Plant biostimulants contain substance(s) and/or microorganisms whose function when applied to plants or the rhizosphere is to stimulate natural processes to enhance/ benefit nutrient uptake, nutrient efficiency, tolerance to abiotic stress, and crop quality. Biostimulants have no direct action against pests, and therefore do not fall within the regulatory framework of pesticides” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012a).

span.label: biostimulant coalition
span.quote: In North America, the biostimulant coalition defined biostimulants as “substances, including microorganisms, that are applied to plant, seed, soil or other growing media that may enhance the plant’s ability to assimilate applied nutrients, or provide benefits to plant development. Biostimulants are not plant nutrients and therefore may not make any nutrient claims or guarantees” (Biostimulant 2013).

span.label: biological control
span.quote: Hence, this definition differentiates plant biostimulants from biological control

span.label: fertilisers
span.quote: Finally, the EBIC concept of biostimulants includes products with some nutrients, provided that the effect on plant growth is not through direct fertilization: “Biostimulants operate through different mechanisms than fertilisers, regardless of the presence of nutrients in the products” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012b).

span.label: root exudates

span.label: phytase

span.label: plant biostimulant - THE EUROPEAN (EBIC) SENSE: defined by FUNCTION and fenced off from pesticides by regulation - substances or microorganisms that stimulate natural processes, with no direct action against pests
span.quote: “Plant biostimulants contain substance(s) and/or microorganisms whose function when applied to plants or the rhizosphere is to stimulate natural processes to enhance/ benefit nutrient uptake, nutrient efficiency, tolerance to abiotic stress, and crop quality. Biostimulants have no direct action against pests, and therefore do not fall within the regulatory framework of pesticides” (European Biostimulants Industry 2012a).

span.label: plant biostimulant - THE NORTH AMERICAN (coalition) SENSE: defined by what it is APPLIED TO and fenced off from fertilisers by claim - may enhance nutrient assimilation, but is not a plant nutrient and may make no nutrient claim. TWO INDUSTRY CONSORTIA, ONE TERM, AND THE BOUNDARY IS DRAWN AGAINST A DIFFERENT NEIGHBOUR ON EACH SIDE OF THE ATLANTIC
span.quote: In North America, the biostimulant coalition defined biostimulants as “substances, including microorganisms, that are applied to plant, seed, soil or other growing media that may enhance the plant’s ability to assimilate applied nutrients, or provide benefits to plant development. span.label: biostimulant - THIS REVIEW'S SCOPE DECISION: a biofertilizer counts as a biostimulant, a boundary other definitions of the same term explicitly deny
span.quote: Microbial inoculants that act as biofertilizers are considered as biostimulants in the present review.

span.label: biofertilizer - a LIVING product, defined by the mechanisms through which it promotes growth rather than by what it contains
span.quote: Biofertilizers are biological products containing living microorganisms that, when applied to seed, plant surfaces, or soil, promote growth by several mechanisms such as increasing the supply of nutrients, increasing root biomass or root area, and increasing nutrient uptake capacity of the plant (Vessey 2003).

span.label: nitrogen fixed by Azospirillum supplied a modest share of wheat nitrogen but the large majority of sugarcane nitrogen - the same mechanism differing by an order of magnitude between crops
span.quote: (Malik et al. 2002), using 15N tracer techniques, found that Azospirillum brasilense and Azospirillum lipoferum contributed between 7–12 % of the total nitrogen content of wheat.

span.label: a three-strain PGPR mixture increased tomato uptake of labelled fertilizer, showing the inoculant changes uptake of applied nutrients and not only of soil ones
span.quote: (Adesemoye et al. 2010) reported that a three-strain mixture of Bacillus spp. PGPR promoted growth of tomato and increased plant uptake of 15N-depleted fertilizer.

span.label: most soil organic phosphorus is present as phytate, which plants cannot take up at all until an enzyme releases it
span.quote: The predominant forms of organic phosphorus are phytates (inositol hexa- and penta-phosphates), which constitute up to 60 % of soil organic phosphorus.

span.label: biofertilizer defined by its mechanisms - increasing nutrient supply, root biomass or area, and uptake capacity

span.label: the share of total plant nitrogen attributable to Azospirillum fixation in wheat against sugarcane

span.label: organic phosphorus as a share of soil phosphorus
span.quote: Organic phosphorus, which is about 30-80 % of soil phosphorus, plays an important role in the phosphorus cycle of agricultural soils (Tarafdar and Gharu 2006).

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-014-2131-8.
